newsitem.title: UK: British Steel pays price of firm pound.
newsitem.headline: British Steel pays price of firm pound.

text.p: British Steel Plc said Monday profits tumbled last year on stiff price competition and the strength of the pound, and announced plans to accelerate job cuts.
Pretax profits fell to 451 million pounds ($737 million) from 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) the previous year. Sales rose 2 percent to 7.2 billion pounds ($11.8 billion).
Sir Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive, admitted the year had been a "difficult" one, but made clear the pound's pain was not over despite brightening prospects in the steel market.
"The steel trading outlook for 1997/98 is one of cautious optimism, although concerns remain about the current strength of sterling and its serious impact on our future profits."

He issued a warning that the pain would be felt across Britain's export industry. A stronger pound makes British exporters' goods less competitive in world markets and makes sales by companies' overseas units worth less at home.

"The strength of sterling is a problem to British Steel and to many of its UK customers who are also significant exporters. Their order books are bound to be affected later this year if sterling remains at its present level," said Moffat.

As a result of the profit collapse, Moffat announced three price-cutting initiatives on Monday. The first is to speed up the job cutting programme. It did not detail job cuts or the potential cost in its latest results statement.
Recent press reports have indicated that the group could cut up to 10,000 jobs in five years, compared with the regular 500 to 1,000 jobs normally shed each year.
A group spokesman told Reuters earlier this year the group would axe "significantly more than 5,000 jobs over five years" at a cost of tens of millions of pounds.
The other two cost cutting drives will be in raw materials, supplies and services and improving use of information technology.

The root of its woes is the pound which has risen more than 20 percent against the mark since last summer leaving companies like British Steel exposed. A big chunk of its sales on the European mainland is denominated in marks.
Some 80 percent of its sales are sterling-sensitive and some 55 percent of sales are generated outside Britain.
The company has also been hurt by stiff price competition in Britain.
The profit slump was in line with analysts' forecasts, but British Steel stock fell 4.75 pence (about 8 cents) to 158.50 pence ($2.59) on the London Stock Exchange.
